title: Gathin23/cleanyourtv
author: Gathin23
body:
**The viral tweet:** [x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102](https://x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102) On 17 October 2026 I posted a before and after of my parents' TV, cleaned up by Claude Code over Wi-Fi. It reached 7.4M views, people started doing the same to their own TVs, and their replies turned into the lists here: 170+ TV models from 200+ contributors in four days. The repo was called tv-vibehack until the 19th; old links work. **Themes, switches and add-ons:** [cleanyour.tv/addons](https://cleanyour.tv/addons) **Official links:** the website is [cleanyour.tv](https://cleanyour.tv) and the code, launcher and tools live only in this repo. Other domains using the name, such as cleanyourtv.com, are not run by this project ([#1004](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/issues/1004)). ## How it works Android TVs have the same debug bridge as Android phones. Switch on USB debugging in the TV's developer options, allow your computer once, and the rest is standard Android tooling: | Step | What happens | |---|---| | **Back up** | The list of installed packages and settings. | | **Disable** | The manufacturer's telemetry, ad services, content rows and preloaded junk, with `pm disable-user`. Nothing is uninstalled, so a restore script can undo every step. | | **Install** | A small native launcher, made the default home screen. | **No root, no cable, nothing uninstalled, and a one-line restore if you change your mind.** The bloat differs by brand, so the prompt has your coding assistant discover it on your TV and ask before touching anything you might use. ## Quick start | You have | Do this | |---|---| | **A computer** | Use the prompt with a coding assistant: the three steps below. | | **Only an Android phone** | Use the community-built [Clean Your TV app](https://cleanyour.tv/app) by [@udhaykumarbala](https://github.com/udhaykumarbala): connect, analyse, clean, in about five minutes. No laptop, no coding agent. | With a computer, you need it on the same Wi-Fi as the TV and a coding assistant with shell access. Any of these work: Claude Code (on [0G Private Computer](https://pc.0g.ai) or an [Anthropic plan](https://claude.com/pricing)), [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) or [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli). | Where | What to do | |---|---| | **1. On the TV** | Settings → Device Preferences → About → press OK on **Build** seven times → back → Developer options → **USB debugging** on. If you see a Network or ADB debugging toggle, turn that on too. Keep the TV on. | | **2. On your computer** | Clone the repo and open that folder in your assistant (`git clone https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv`), then paste [`PROMPT.md`](PROMPT.md) and fill in your TV model. | | **3. Follow along** | Accept "Allow USB debugging?" on the TV, then answer the checklist: which apps you use, the dock size and app order, whether to keep the voice assistant, Chromecast and updates. | Cloning matters: the assistant reuses this repo's `tools/disable.sh` and `launcher/build-and-install.sh` instead of writing its own, and that is where the backup, the Home guard and the restore record live. The assistant backs up, debloats, builds and installs the launcher, and checks each step with screenshots pulled from the TV. With this repo as context it takes about fifteen minutes. ## What you get A home screen that looks like an Apple TV and gets out of the way: | Part | What it looks like | |---|---| | **A pitch-black home** | A dock of your four favourite apps in a rounded band, where Apple TV puts it. | | **A top shelf** | Names the focused app in large type, with an ambient glow in a colour taken from its artwork. | | **The rest of your apps in a grid** | Slides up when you press Down. | | **One floating glass highlight** | Springs from tile to tile. The focused tile lifts and shows its name. | | **Three frosted buttons** | Inputs (HDMI ports under the names you gave them in the TV's settings, AV, Live TV), Wi-Fi or Ethernet with the network name, Settings. | | **A greeting, a thin clock and the date** | In [Outfit](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Outfit), and a matching Clock screensaver. Set `show_stats` in config or a theme for one line under the clock: CPU, free memory and free storage. It stays off unless you turn it on, and it refreshes only while Home is on screen. | | **Themes and module cards** | Themes change colours, wallpaper, dock and columns without a rebuild, and module cards let other apps plug a tile in, only with your say-so. | And a TV that stops working against you: no sponsored rows, no "Discover" nags, no analytics phoning home, no apps you never asked for. | | | |---|---| | ![The top shelf names the focused app over an ambient glow in its colour](docs/focus-2-up-netflix.png) | ![The Inputs popup: HDMI ports with what is connected, AV and Live TV](docs/inputs-menu.jpg) | | *Top shelf and ambient glow* | *Inputs: HDMI with connection state, AV, Live TV* | | ![The grid with the glass highlight on a tile and its name beneath](docs/focus-1-fancode.png) | ![The Clock screensaver: a thin clock drifting over the glow](docs/clock-screensaver.png) | | *The grid, one glass highlight, the tile's name* | *Clock screensaver, drifts so nothing burns in* | | ![The aurora theme: a wallpaper and tinted pills, pushed without a rebuild](themes/aurora/screenshot.jpg) | ![Six columns and a six-app dock from a theme's config.json](themes/six-columns/screenshot.jpg) | | *Aurora theme, pushed with `tools/theme.sh`* | *Six columns and a six-app dock, same launcher* | | ![Moving a tile: held OK, chose Move, the tile is picked up and the others dim](docs/tile-move.jpg) | ![The App library: installed apps, one press adds an app back to Home](docs/app-library.jpg) | | *With `tile_menu`, hold OK on a tile, Move: arrows carry it, Back puts it down* | *App library: one press puts a removed app back on Home* | ## Supported TVs Anything running **Android TV** or **Google TV**. | Platform | What works | |---|---| | **Android TV, Google TV** | The debloat and the launcher. | | **Fire TV** | The debloat half only, since Fire OS will not hand Home to a third-party launcher. And on the 2015 Fire TV Box (Fire OS 5) even that half fails: every `pm` route is refused. | | **A few China-market TCL sets** | They refuse to install any launcher at all; their lists say so in the header. | | **Samsung (Tizen), LG (webOS)** | Different systems. See [SHOWCASE.md](SHOWCASE.md#other-platforms-fire-tv-and-lg-webos) for three webOS ports, and [docs/devices/samsung-tizen.md](docs/devices/samsung-tizen.md) for what a 2021 Samsung set answers over Wi-Fi (no ADB, so no `pm disable-user`) if you are weighing a Tizen port. | Tested lists from contributors, one folder per model in [`examples/`](examples/): **TCL** 65 · **Sony** 37 · **Xiaomi** 31 · **Philips** 16 · **Hisense** 10 · **Skyworth** 10 · **Amazon Fire TV** 7 · **BenQ** 4 · **OnePlus** 4 · **Panasonic** 4 · **Thomson** 4 · **Google** 3 · **Haier** 3 · **JVC** 3 · **SHARP** 3 · **Vu** 3 · **CHiQ** 2 · **FFalcon** 2 · **Hitachi** 2 · **Insignia Fire TV** 2 · **Kalley** 2 · **Kogan** 2 · **Motorola** 2 · **Nokia** 2 · **NVIDIA Shield** 2 · **onn** 2 · **RCA** 2 · **Redmi** 2 · **RockTek** 2 · **Sankey** 2 · **Toshiba** 2 · **Vidda** 2 · Acer · AiPro2K · AIWA · AQUA · Artel · ASUS · Beko · Caxium · Cecotec · Challenger · Compac · Dcolor · Dialog · EKO · Freebox · Grundig · INCLO · Karbonn · KTC · Liberton · Lumio · Master-G · MTC · Next · Noblex · OK. · Panavox · PEAQ · Polytron · PRISM+ · SANYO · Sber · Super General · Tele System · TiVo · Tornado · Turkcell · Tuvio · Verizon · Vision · Alwtniet, Anker Nebula, BYINTEK, Epson, Formovie, Gadnic, HOTACK, HY320, JMGO, Magcubic, Portronics, Stellamore, Wanbo and XGIMI projectors

Windows (PowerShell) Every script has a PowerShell twin next to it. On Windows with Android Studio installed nothing else is needed: ```powershell python -m venv tools\venv; tools\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r tools\requirements.txt powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File launcher\build-and-install.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\disable.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 examples\xiaomi-mi-tv-4a\debloat.txt ```
How the scripts protect Home The install scripts ask the TV which launcher owns Home and only disable one they recognise, the four in `KNOWN_STOCK_LAUNCHERS`: `com.google.android.tvlauncher`, `com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx`, `com.google.android.leanbacklauncher` and Xiaomi's `com.mitv.tvhome` (PatchWall). Pass `STOCK_LAUNCHER=` (`-StockLauncher`) to override, or `none` to leave it alone. `tools/disable.sh` (`disable.ps1`) applies the same rule before it disables anything: if the list contains the app that owns Home and no other app on the TV answers HOME, it skips that entry, says why, and disables the rest of the list. The setup wizard, the settings apps, a vendor `FallbackHome` and factory-test apps (Xiaomi's `com.duokan.factorytest`) answer HOME too and don't count. So a list applied before the launcher handover cannot leave the TV with nothing to start. Run the same list again once `launcher/build-and-install.sh` has made the new launcher Home and the entry is applied; `FORCE_HOME=1` (`$env:FORCE_HOME`) disables it anyway.
Where your lists can live Debloat list paths passed to `disable.sh` and `restore.sh` are relative to the directory you run from, so your own lists can live outside the repository. Absolute paths also work.
## The microphone, and what can be said about it "Which of these packages is listening?" has no honest one-line answer, and a permission scan makes it worse: on many sets most packages run as `android.uid.system`, so fifty of them show `RECORD_AUDIO: granted=true` and none of them record anything. On others the microphone is in the remote, not the panel, and a package with no audio permission at all still sees everything on screen — ACR clients such as `tv.inscape.tvclient.inscapeacr` identify content from the picture and need only `INTERNET`. `tools/privacy.py` reports what the TV actually says instead of guessing: `TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/privacy.py` prints voice, ACR and telemetry candidates in three groups, each with its evidence — named by the firmware's own `voice_interaction_service`, a known component from [`examples/`](examples/), or nothing but a matching name — plus whether the package declares `RECORD_AUDIO`, whether it shares the system UID, and whether the returned AppOps history contains microphone access. A configured mode or a rejected attempt alone is not evidence of access. `--write privacy.txt` turns the identified candidates into a normal debloat list, so applying it and undoing it are the commands you already use (`tools/disable.sh`, `tools/restore.sh`). Packages that only matched by name stay out unless you pass `--include-low`; they are the ones to check with `dumpsys package ` first. What the audit cannot do is prove intent. `appops` shows an op was touched, not what happened to the stream afterwards, and no scan of package names proves a TV is or is not recording. Disabling an assistant is a trade you make with a specific loss (the remote's mic button, voice search inside apps), which is why the report names that loss per package instead of calling it a win. ## The launcher A small native home screen for Android TV: **about 518 KB**, plain Java, built for TVs with 1 GB of RAM. Themes set the same keys plus a background colour and a wallpaper.

Hold OK on it for its menu: **Launcher settings** (with `launcher_settings_button` a click opens those instead and the menu leaves the row out), **Native settings** where the TV ships a settings app of its own beside Android's - Xiaomi China, TCL/FFALCON and Fire OS are in `settings_fallback_components` - because that app holds pages Android's has no row for, such as Xiaomi's Account & Security with the ADB switch; **Module cards** with `module_cards`; **Edit dock** with `dock_row`; and **Reorder apps**. The launcher's own page has these rows, top to bottom: - **Reorder apps**, only with `launcher_settings_button`: OK picks an app up, the arrows move it, Back places it, and Back again finishes. - **Apps per row** 4, 5, 6 or 7; **Rows below dock** 0 to 3, how many rows of tiles stay visible under the dock band; **Dock band opacity** 100%, 70%, 50% or 30%. The last two only do anything while the dock is its own row (`dock_row`, on by default). - **Wallpaper**: one picture from the theme's collection (or its `wallpaper.jpg`), **None**, or **Theme default**. A pick holds that picture and stops the rotation until you choose Theme default, press Follow theme, or push the theme again. - **Animations** on or off, and **Advanced effects** (tile lift, icon zoom and smooth ambient-colour transitions; they may use more memory) once animations are on. - **Open on start**, only with `open_on_start_choice`: Off, or an app that opens instead of Home the first time Home comes up after the TV starts. Once per boot, so Home and Back still reach the launcher. - **Follow theme (reset on-TV choices)**, which clears every choice above. Pushing or resetting a theme clears them too. - **Choose default home** opens Android's home picker, and **TV system settings** the TV's own settings page. - **Change the default home:** Launcher settings and the optional Default-home tile (`show_home_settings_shortcut`) open Android's home picker. Choose the original launcher to stop using CleanYourTV as Home, or CleanYourTV to return. The original launcher must be enabled; if the install script disabled it, run the restore script below first. Some TVs provide no home picker.
Languages English, German, Danish, Spanish, Catalan, French, Russian, Serbian (Latin), Polish, Czech, Italian, Portuguese, Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese (Taiwan), Thai, Finnish, Vietnamese, Bangla, Indonesian, Norwegian Bokmål, Dutch, Uzbek (Latin), Ukrainian and Korean. The launcher follows the TV's language. Android 13+ can set it for the launcher alone: `tools/tv.py 'cmd locale set-app-locales com.gathin.tvhome --locales ca'`. Hebrew mirrors the layout: menu buttons on the left, date and clock on the right with the greeting above, dock and app rows starting on the right with matching remote navigation, the input selector's icons and labels on the right, and dates with the month prefix ב (for example, 19 באוקטובר). The Clock screensaver right-aligns its date and time. Russian covers every screen, including race weekends, festival greetings and the Shamsi date. Other languages keep their original layouts.
Module cards Any TV app can declare its own tile (label, caption, glow). The launcher asks you once per app, keeps it hidden by default, and remembers the answer for that app's signing key and card name. Hold OK on Settings and choose Module cards to change your mind. How to make one: [`docs/modules.md`](docs/modules.md); the contract: [`docs/specs/card.md`](docs/specs/card.md).
Clock screensaver Pick "Clock" in the TV's screensaver settings, or over ADB: ```bash tools/tv.py 'settings put secure screensaver_components com.gathin.tvhome/.ClockDream; settings put secure screensaver_enabled 1' ```
Remote keys - An optional accessibility service keeps the remote's **Input** button working on Google TV (`INPUT_KEY_SERVICE=1` at install). - It can bring back other buttons only the stock launcher answered, such as the **YouTube** button (`app_keys` and `input_key_keycodes`, in config.xml or a theme; `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` reads `app_keys` too). - A `hold:` prefix on an `app_keys` entry gives that button a second app: a normal press opens the unprefixed app, holding for half a second opens the hold one (by keycode or `hold:scan:...`). - In place of an app, an `app_keys` entry can name an action: `back`, `home`, `recents`, `mute`, `sleep`, `screensaver`, `settings` or `wifi`, so a spare colour button can mute the TV or, held, put it in standby. - `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` also fixes sticks whose Home key sends ALL_APPS, and opens Settings from the remote's **gear** button, even one Android does not map (scancodes or keycodes in config.xml). - With `settings_key_panel` the gear opens a [small quick settings panel](docs/quick-settings-panel.jpg) over Home or any app: TV settings, Display, Network, Apps and Launcher settings.
Navigation and artwork Up and Down move one row. The top buttons never fall through to tiles, and Down from them returns to the dock tile you came from. The last focused app is remembered, and installing or removing an app refreshes the tiles while Home is open. App banners load at xhdpi or better, so low-density TV UIs do not downsample them before the focus zoom.
## Restoring your TV Keep the list you applied. One line puts the TV back the way it was: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt # Android TV TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx # Google TV ``` | What | How | |---|---| | **A record comes first** | Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like, in `~/.cleanyourtv/`. | | **Restore replays it** | A package you had disabled yourself stays disabled, and Home goes back to the component that owned it. | | **The launcher stays installed** | Remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone. | | **No computer?** | If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too. |
What the record holds, and what happens without one Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like: for every package in the list whether it was enabled, already disabled or not installed, which component owned Home, and the three animation scales. That record lives in `~/.cleanyourtv/`, one file per TV and list, and a second run of the same list keeps the first record instead of saving the cleaned-up state over it. If you added packages to the list since, that run adds them to the record before disabling them. Keep the list you applied. The restore script replays the record, so a package you had disabled yourself stays disabled and Home goes back to the component that owned it: The `stock launcher` argument is only a fallback: with a record, the launcher that actually owned Home is the one that gets it back, and the argument is used only when nothing answered HOME at the time or this project's launcher owned it. The stock launcher is enabled again either way, unless it was already disabled when the record was taken. Without a record (an older run, or a record you deleted) the script says so and falls back to enabling the whole list and resetting the scales to `1.0`, which is what it used to do. It leaves the new launcher installed (remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone) and does not know about packages you disabled outside the list. To switch back later, run the install script again; it works out which launcher to disable even when Home has fallen back to Android's chooser. If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too.
## After a firmware update An update installs over the cleaned-up system: the listed packages come back, Home goes to the stock launcher, and new preloads appear that no list mentions. Nothing else here notices, so compare the TV with the list you applied: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` It exits with `0` when the TV still matches the list, `1` when something drifted, and `2` when it could not check at all: the TV did not answer, nobody accepted the "Allow USB debugging?" prompt in time, the list path is not there, or the list disables Android's core packages. Only 1 is drift, so a job that mails on 1 alone stays quiet while the check never ran; mail on anything but 0, or on 2 as well, and a weekly job on a home server or a Pi is enough to hear about it: ```bash 0 9 * * 1 cd ~/cleanyourtv && TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` `TV_HOST` is read before any of that: a run that leaves it unset stops in `tools/tv.py` with its own message and also exits 1, so set it in the job line, as above, where cron does not inherit it from your shell. `--fix` reapplies the list to what drifted: it switches Home to the launcher the list does not disable (pass a package as the second argument if you run a fork), then disables the listed packages that came back, and reads the TV back to confirm both. It writes no recovery record, because the record already holds the state from before the first run: `tools/restore.sh` still returns the TV to stock afterwards. Home is fixed first; if no launcher is left to take it, `--fix` changes nothing and says so. It runs the same safety checks as `tools/disable.sh` before it disables anything, since an update is the moment they matter again: it leaves setupwraith on while the saved Wi-Fi network belongs to it (`FORCE_SETUPWRAITH=1` on Ethernet), leaves the packages under the HDMI/AV inputs on (`TVINPUT_ALLOW=1` if you really want them off), leaves on the apps the TV opens its inputs and Settings with (`HANDLERS_ALLOW=1`), and never takes Home to a vendor `FallbackHome` or a factory-test app. Each package it leaves on comes with the reason and exits 1, because the TV is not back to the list until you deal with that one by hand. With `stock_home_redirect` the stock launcher can stay Home on purpose: the list leaves it out, the install script ran with `STOCK_LAUNCHER=none`, Android keeps it as Home, and `HomeKeyService` sends its home screen on to this launcher. On the Chromecast with Google TV 4K that setup matches the folder's `debloat-keep-cast.txt`, not its `debloat.txt`, which disables setupwraith and the screensaver pair the redirect setup keeps. On the Acer AR55AR2851UDPRO it is the folder's `debloat.txt`. Check those lists with the stock launcher as the second argument. title: Zagitta/gpu-unlock
author: Zagitta
body:
# GPU unlock 1.0.0

Unlock FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards to their professional equivalents

This Linux kernel module combines the CMP unlocker's V67/PLM technique with the pre-driver timing of the UEFI approach. It runs the unlock, writes the speed selectors (SS0 `0x88888888`, which selects the full BF16 rate, and the 4-bit SS1 `0x8` IMLA4) and performs FLR before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds the card. It is neither a UEFI application nor a patched NVIDIA driver. 

The benefit of this early kmod driver is that it does not require manual patching each time nvidia releases a new driver version.

The effect of this unlock is that it doubles the instruction issuing speed of FP/BF16 FMA into FP32 operations on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards.

[3090 Ti dense 8192³ GEMM at 450 W, five-sample medians with FP32 accumulation](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/1#issue-5905622687):


| Input | Before       | After         |
| ----- | ------------ | ------------- |
| FP16  | 87.46 TFLOPS | 118.39 TFLOPS |
| BF16  | 87.50 TFLOPS | 157.41 TFLOPS |
| TF32  | 42.58 TFLOPS | 82.61 TFLOPS  |

## Tested cards

Results reported by users. The module accepts every GeForce ID listed in
`kernel/gpu_unlock/main.c`, but the cards below are the ones someone has
reported on. Please add yours with a
[compatibility report](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/new?template=compatibility-report.yml),
whether it worked or not.

| Chip  | Card                              | PCI ID      | Result                              | BF16 GEMM gain | Reports |
| ----- | --------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------- | ------- |
| GA102 | RTX 3090 Ti                       | `10de:2203` | Unlocked                            | +68–80%        | [#1](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/1) |
| GA102 | RTX 3090                          | `10de:2204` | Unlocked                            | +25–67%        | [#5](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/5), [#9](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/9), [#10](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/10), [#17](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/17), [#25](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/25), [#27](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/27), [#33](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/33) |
| GA102 | RTX 3080 Ti 20 GB (OEM, GA102-250) | `10de:2205` | Unlock completes, BF16 stays at half rate | —        | [#28](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/28) |
| GA102 | RTX 3080 10 GB                    | `10de:2206` | Unlocked                            | +70–73%        | [#14](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/14) |
| GA102 | RTX 3080 20 GB (memory upgrade)   | `10de:2206` | Unlocked                            | +56–59%        | [#10](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/10), [#15](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/15) |
| GA104 | RTX 3070                          | `10de:2484` | Unlocked                            | +73–81%        | [#10](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/10), [#12](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/12) |
| GA104 | RTX 3070 Ti                       | `10de:2482` | Not tested with this module (the same unlock worked from a UEFI port on Windows) | — | [#32](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/32) |
| GA106 | RTX 3060 12 GB                    | `10de:2504` | Unlocked                            | about +80%     | [#13](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/pull/13), [#31](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/31) |
| GA103 | any                               | `10de:2414` | No reports yet                      | —              | — |

The gains are dense GEMM throughput from each report's own benchmark, so
they are not directly comparable. The power limit matters a lot: the lowest
figure (+25%) is from cards capped at 225 W.

Matrix-heavy work speeds up: LLM prefill (+14–36% in
[#9](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/9),
[#15](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/15),
[#25](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/25) and
[#33](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/33)), diffusion and
FlashAttention. LLM decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth, and INT8
work stay about the same. The reports that compared outputs found them
bit-identical before and after.

Reports also cover up to four cards in one machine, the card driving the
display, and cards passed through to a VM with vfio-pci
([#17](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/17)).




## How to install

First run:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock
cd gpu-unlock
make install
```

Then append `gpu_unlock.targets=all` to your kernel command line, keeping
existing options:

- **GRUB (Debian/Ubuntu/Mint):** add it inside `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`
in `/etc/default/grub`, then run `sudo update-grub`.
- **GRUB (Arch/CachyOS):** same edit, then run
`sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg`.
- **Fedora/RHEL:** run
`sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="gpu_unlock.targets=all"`.
- **systemd-boot:** append it to the `options` line in your boot entry
(`bootctl status` shows its location).
- **UKI / generated entries:** add it to `/etc/kernel/cmdline` and regenerate
your boot images/entries (e.g. `sudo mkinitcpio -P` for mkinitcpio UKIs).



## Local build

Every build downloads the pinned NVIDIA/CachyOS inputs over HTTPS, checks
their SHA-256, and generates firmware only in the build directory and the
binary package. All three formats install through the same `make install-*`
targets. Packages are built from the committed `HEAD`.

Build, install build dependencies, and install the packages in one step
(asks for your sudo password):

```sh
make install        # detect the distribution and select an installer
make install-arch   # makepkg -sif
make install-deb    # apt-get build-dep, dpkg-buildpackage, apt-get install
make install-rpm    # dnf builddep, rpmbuild, dnf install
```

`make install` uses `/etc/os-release` (`ID`, then `ID_LIKE`) to detect Arch,
Debian/Ubuntu, or Fedora/RHEL/CentOS families. The RPM installer requires DNF.
For other distributions, select a compatible explicit target above.

`make arch`, `make deb` and `make rpm` only build. Debian and RPM packages go
to `build/deb` and `build/rpm`. The NVIDIA inputs are cached in
`~/.cache/gpu-unlock/inputs` (`make inputs`; override with `INPUTS=`).
`dpkg-buildpackage` itself never uses the network, so a clean-chroot build (sbuild or
pbuilder) needs `GPU_UNLOCK_INPUTS` pointing at that cache.
The `make dist` archive, the Debian source package and the `.nosrc.rpm`
contain no NVIDIA archives or generated firmware.

## Boot flow and opt-in

The packages put `gpu_unlock` and its firmware in the initramfs and load it
there, before `nvidia` can bind a card:

- **mkinitcpio:** `/etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/zz-gpu-unlock.conf` inserts
`gpu_unlock` right before `nvidia` in `MODULES`, so a display card is blank
for as short a time as possible. Without `nvidia` in the image, it goes
last and still runs before an `nvidia` loaded from the root filesystem.
Images are rebuilt on install. mkinitcpio ignores drop-ins for an image
built with `-c <config>` or a preset `_config`; put `gpu_unlock` right
before `nvidia` in that config's `MODULES` yourself.
- **initramfs-tools:** `/usr/share/initramfs-tools/modules.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.
- **dracut:** `/usr/lib/dracut/dracut.conf.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.

With initramfs-tools and dracut, the module is built for every installed
kernel that has headers, and those kernels' images are rebuilt on install
and again on removal. Kernels installed later get the module and a new
image from the kernel's own install hooks.

There is no `softdep nvidia pre:` rule: kmod honours only the first
`softdep nvidia` line it reads, so other packages' rules (`nvidia-utils`,
`gddr6_hwmon`) would silently override it, or it would override theirs.

The module does nothing unless the kernel command line opts in:

```
gpu_unlock.targets=all                          # every unbound GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0                 # only these cards
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0,0000:22:00.0    # comma-separated
```

Addresses are full PCI names as `lspci -D` prints them (hex digits in either
case), independent of GPU numbering and display role. An entry that is not
a GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card, including `all` mixed with addresses, is logged and ignored.
The cards are unlocked concurrently, about a second in all however many
there are, and each on its own: a card that is already bound or powered
down is skipped. Bus mastering that the board firmware left on (Supermicro
X11 does this whatever its option ROM and bus master settings) is cleared
first; a card some driver already initialised is still refused. Then
`nvidia` loads and binds every card as usual.

The display card works too. Its firmware framebuffer (the boot console and
Plymouth) keeps running while the unlock's firmware steps run, and is
removed just before the card's reset, as `nvidia-drm` would do a moment
later anyway. Its screen is blank from that reset until `nvidia-drm` takes
over.

Loading the module by hand after boot does nothing to a card that `nvidia`
has bound.

Suspend to RAM powers the cards off, which resets the speed selectors. After
resume the module unlocks every card it unlocked at boot again, before
`nvidia` resumes it: its suspend notifier runs just ahead of the one `nvidia`
resumes its cards from (`NVreg_UseKernelSuspendNotifiers=1`, the default in
current drivers; `nvidia-resume.service` runs later still). This adds about a
second to resume. A card that kept power, as in suspend to idle, is still
unlocked and is only read. A card that `nvidia` has already resumed, or that is
bound to another driver, is left as it is, and the log says why. Add
`gpu_unlock.resume=0` to the kernel command line, or write `0` to
`/sys/module/gpu_unlock/parameters/resume`, to turn this off. Hibernation is
not covered.

Check the result with:

```sh
journalctl -k -b | grep gpu_unlock
lspci -nnk -s 0000:21:00.0
```

To stop unlocking, remove `gpu_unlock.targets=` from the kernel command line;
for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the
packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.

If the firmware on a card never stops, the module logs it and keeps the DMA
buffers that firmware may still use until the next power off. Power off
before trying again.

The kernel module and local packaging are GPL-2.0-only. The generated payload
derives from the pinned CMP reference; NVIDIA firmware remains under its own
terms. See `firmware/NOTICE.md` and `licenses/` for attribution and notices.

# MacNativeGames

Play your own Tears of the Kingdom and Breath of the Wild natively on Apple silicon Mac, iPhone and iPad.
Not an emulator: the game's own ARM64 code runs directly on Apple chips, and its NVN graphics are rebuilt on Metal.

# English **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0 and 1.9.0 are now officially supported on Mac!** 1.6.0 also runs on the iPhone (first played on an iPhone 14, October 23). **Tears of the Kingdom 1.0.0, 1.2.1 and 1.4.3 are now officially supported on Mac, iPhone and iPad!** > **Use your AI assistant to help you build the Mac app. We recommend Claude Code, Codex, or any other AI assistant you prefer.** [English](#english) | [中文](#chinese) ## Legal **You must own the game.** Use this project only with a copy of The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom that you bought, and with keys and system files dumped from your own Nintendo Switch. This is an independent, non-commercial project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Nintendo. The Legend of Zelda and Nintendo Switch are trademarks of Nintendo. The repository contains no game content and distributes none: no game program, art, text, audio, shaders or keys. Everything the game needs is made on your own computer from your own files when you build the app. The app you build contains the game, so it is for your own use only; do not share it. What the repository does hold is the information needed to make the port work: the patch code, the addresses and hashes used to check your files, and the [shared shader list](docs/shader-list.md), which names shaders and bind states but contains no shader code. Play your own copy of **The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom** natively on Apple silicon Mac, iPhone, and iPad. Bring your game file (XCI or NSP) and your `prod.keys`; one script builds a Mac app or an unsigned iPhone/iPad IPA. The iOS build requires iOS/iPadOS 26 and iPhone 14 or newer. It is not an emulator: the game's own ARM64 code runs directly on Apple chips (rewritten where the operating system requires it), the Switch system services are answered by a small host, and the game's NVN graphics are rebuilt on Metal. Nothing from the game is in this repository, and the project is not affiliated with Nintendo. Version 1.4.3 has been played on an iPhone 14 and an iPad; see [iPhone and iPad](docs/install.md#iphone-and-ipad). ## Let's maintain the shader list together: no more stutter > [!TIP] > **Every shader in the shared list is ready before you play.** On a Mac the game does not stop to compile it, and on an iPhone or iPad nothing is missing from the picture. The more places players cover, the smoother the game gets for everyone. The [shared shader list](docs/shader-list.md) now holds **34,937 shader variants** (28,464 shaders) from the Mac, iPhone and iPad: only states a build does not make by itself, since every build makes each shader's default variant. Every build makes them from the player's own game files, so the list holds identifiers only, never game data. Helping takes no setup: 1. **Play.** Every build carries each shader of the game for its default bind state. When your game meets a shader in a state that variant does not serve, or builds a render pipeline the app's list lacks, it notes it in `shader-list-contribution.txt`; default variants are never noted. 2. **On a Mac, every 100 new rows (shaders and pipelines together) it asks you once, before the game starts.** Click "Send": the GitHub form opens and the file is shown, ready to drag in. If the GitHub CLI (`gh`) is installed and signed in, the dialog offers "Submit automatically" instead, which sends this batch for you (a private gist and an issue) without opening the browser. An iPhone or iPad never asks during play: while it is connected to the Mac that built its app (cable or the same Wi-Fi), the Mac asks instead. "Don't remind me again" stops the reminders. 3. **Everyone's next build carries them.** Nobody stutters there again. **[Send your shaders →](https://github.com/ly05010419/MacNativeGames/issues/new?template=shader-list.yml)** · The game never uploads anything by itself. Update history: | Date | Platform | Update | |---|---|---| | Oct 23 | iPhone | **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0** on the iPhone: full screen, add-on content, saves copied from the Mac; both games render at 960x540 on the phone and use their own upscale to 1280x720 (no MetalFX) | | Oct 23 | Mac | **Super Mario Odyssey 1.3.0** (community port, early): Cap Kingdom and Bonneton playable at 60 fps on an M3, own runtime in [`games/odyssey`](games/odyssey/README.md), which has the build steps | | Oct 23 | iPhone, iPad | **Tears of the Kingdom** fills the screen, 60 fps by default, MetalFX upscaling | | Oct 23 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0**: key 2 interpolates again, and Link no longer shakes at 30+30; key 3 switches to native 2K; key 4 (21:9 ultrawide) and key 5 (edge smoothing) now work; every shader is prepared at build time, so far fewer translate in play | | Oct 23 | Mac | **Tears of the Kingdom** renders its 3D scene at the canvas resolution: internal 1920x1080 at 1080p (docked was only 1600x900), 2560x1440 on the 2K canvas | | Oct 21 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.9.0**: shaders and render pipelines optimised | | Oct 21 | Mac, iPhone, iPad | **Tears of the Kingdom**: steadier at 90 fps, and steadier frame rates when no shaders are cached at all | | Oct 20 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.9.0** (early): a base NSP and the 1.9.0 update NSP build the same app, each DLC pack optional (`--dlc`) | | Oct 20 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0** (early): a card image holding the base game, the update and the add-on content builds its own app with the same command; body:
# Free My TV **A fast, ad-free home screen for Google TV, LG and Samsung TVs.** Trending picks from your own apps, the weather at a glance, and a look that follows the sunset.
Open source. Built with Claude Code. One button to undo. [**freemytv.io**](https://freemytv.io) · [Install](#install) · [LG TVs](#lg-tvs-webos) · [Samsung TVs](#samsung-tvs-tizen) · [Any TV](#any-tv) · [Make it yours](#make-it-yours)
## What you get - **No ads.** No sponsored rows, banners or autoplaying promos. Not one. - **Your apps, front and center.** The streaming apps you actually use, on a glass shelf. Pick them and their order right on the TV. - **Trending, not sponsored.** Three fresh picks every hour from what's trending this week and the latest releases, only from apps you already have. Movies and Shows get their own tabs. - **Weather and markets, one press away.** The hour-by-hour forecast (or the next 5 days), sunrise and sunset, and live crypto prices. - **Light by day, dark by night.** It follows your city's real sunset, the way your phone does. - **A screensaver to match.** Full-screen photos of the picks with a big glass clock. - **Your own photos** (Google TV and Android TV). Send them from your computer (up to 100): the screensaver shows them, and without picks one is the home screen's background each hour. - **Fast.** 60 fps, every frame in 16.6 ms, on the TV's own chip. The home screen uses 96 MB of memory instead of 242 MB (−60%).
Measured on a 98″ TCL Google TV running Android 14. - **Set up on the TV.** Language, your city, temperature, theme, the weather and prices cards, the forecast's hours or days, which coins, and the apps on the shelf, in Free My TV's own settings. - **Safe.** No root. Nothing is uninstalled. One button brings back the factory home screen. ## Install About ten minutes. You need a Google TV or Android TV (Android 8 or newer) and a computer on the same Wi-Fi. ### The easy way: an AI assistant 1. **On the TV**, turn on developer mode: Settings → System → About → press *Android TV OS build* 7 times. Then Settings → System → Developer options → turn on **USB debugging**. Write down the TV's IP address (Settings → Network & Internet). 2. **On your computer**, open an AI coding assistant ([Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code), Codex or Antigravity) and say: > Install Free My TV (github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv) on my TV at 192.168.1.50. I live in Lisbon. It downloads the code, installs the tools it needs, builds the app and puts it on your TV, and asks before anything important. Swap in your TV's IP and your city. 3. **On the TV**, open *Free My TV* → *Home Screen* → *Free My TV*. That's when the TV asks *Allow USB debugging?* for Free My TV: tick *Always allow* and accept. ### The ready APK No tools to install besides adb. The APK on the [latest release](https://github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv/releases/latest) has no TMDB key, so the home screen has no picks, and it takes your city from the TV's time zone (change it in *Home Settings* → *City*). 1. **On the TV**, do step 1 above. 2. **On your computer**, download `FreeMyTV.apk` from the release and install it: ```bash adb connect 192.168.1.50:5555 adb install -r FreeMyTV.apk ``` On Android 14, Google Play Protect may hold the install with *Risky app blocked*: choose *More details* → *Install anyway*. 3. **On the TV**, do step 3 above. If you built Free My TV yourself before, switch back to *Original* and uninstall it first: your build and the release are signed with different keys. For the picks, build it yourself with your TMDB key (below). ### The manual way 1. **On the TV**, do step 1 above. 2. **Tools:** a JDK (17+), the Android SDK command-line tools (build-tools 34, platform android-34) and adb. On a Mac: ```bash brew install --cask temurin android-commandlinetools android-platform-tools sdkmanager "build-tools;34.0.0" "platforms;android-34" ``` On Linux, get OpenJDK 17, Android's command-line tools and adb from your package manager, then run the same `sdkmanager` line. On Windows, use Git Bash (which Claude Code uses there) or WSL. 3. **Build:** ```bash ./build.sh ``` The first run creates `config.properties`. Set your city and your [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key) there, then run it again. 4. **Install:** ```bash adb connect 192.168.1.50:5555 adb install -r FreeMyTV.apk ``` If the install seems stuck, look at the TV: on Android 14, Google Play Protect may hold it with *Risky app blocked* ("built for an older version of Android"), since Free My TV targets Android 13. Choose *More details* → *Install anyway*. Updates don't ask again. Chromecast with Google TV on Android 14 keeps port 5555 closed even with USB debugging on: turn on *Wireless debugging* (Developer options), pair with `adb pair `, then run `adb tcpip 5555` over that connection. Port 5555 closes again at every restart, so after one, *Original*, the watchdog and the boot check can't reach ADB until you run `adb tcpip 5555` again (the pairing stays). On TCL TVs, also let it run in the background (TCL blocks it by default, and the switch never starts): ```bash adb shell "appops set io.freemytv AUTO_START allow || appops set io.freemytv APP_AUTO_START allow" ``` 5. **On the TV**, open *Free My TV* → *Home Screen* → *Free My TV*. The TV asks *Allow USB debugging?* once more, now for Free My TV itself: tick *Always allow* and accept. (Run `adb disconnect 192.168.1.50:5555` first: on Android 8 to 10 the TV can hand that answer to a computer that's still connected.) ## LG TVs (webOS) The same home screen as an LG app: the picks, the glass shelf with your apps, the drawer with inputs, weather and prices, day and night, Home Settings and the shelf editor. It installs through LG's own Developer Mode, with nothing rooted or changed on the TV. LG's home screen stays where it is, and Free My TV is one press of a number key away (or in LG's app list, on remotes without them). You need an LG TV (webOS 3 or newer) and a computer on the same Wi-Fi, with Python 3. 1. **On the TV**, open the LG Content Store and install **Developer Mode**. Sign in with a free [LG developer account](https://webostv.developer.lge.com), turn on **Dev Mode Status** (the TV restarts), then turn on **Key Server**. Write down the IP address and the passphrase it shows. 2. **On your computer**, get the code and build. `config.properties` works as for Google TV (your city, your [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key)): ```bash git clone https://github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv && cd free-my-tv python3 webos/build.py ``` 3. **Install.** The first time, it asks for the TV's passphrase; updates don't: ```bash python3 webos/install.py 192.168.1.50 ``` 4. **On the TV**, while Free My TV is open, hold a number key on the remote. From then on, that key opens it from anywhere. On a remote without number keys, open it from LG's app list on the home screen, like any other app. With an AI assistant, say *"Install Free My TV (github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv) on my LG TV at 192.168.1.50. I live in Lisbon."* It builds the app and hands you the install command, so you type the passphrase yourself. With the [webOS Homebrew Channel](https://github.com/webosbrew/webos-homebrew-channel), you can skip the computer: add the repository `https://freemytv.io/webos/apps.json` in the Channel's settings, and Free My TV shows up in its list. That's the release build: it takes the city from the TV's time zone, and the picks need your own build with a [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key). If you installed your own build, don't update it from there, or the release replaces it. On webOS 6 and newer, LG doesn't let apps installed through Developer Mode see which apps the TV has. Free My TV then shows the well-known ones it finds (Netflix, YouTube, Prime Video, Disney+, Apple TV, Plex and more) and asks the TV, once, for the access LG's phone app uses: a message on the TV asks whether to allow Free My TV. Allow it, and from the next start all your apps show, with their icons. Developer Mode lasts about 40 days: open the Developer Mode app now and then and press **EXTEND**. To remove Free My TV, run `python3 webos/install.py 192.168.1.50 --uninstall`. ## Samsung TVs (Tizen) The same home screen as a Samsung app, with everything the LG one has: the picks, the shelf, the drawer with the inputs, the weather and the prices, day and night, and its own settings. It installs through Samsung's own Developer Mode, with nothing rooted or changed on the TV, and Samsung's home screen stays where it is. You need a Samsung TV from 2017 or newer (Tizen 3+) and a computer on the same Wi-Fi. (2015 and 2016 models, on Orsay or Tizen 2, can't run it; a Google TV streamer on HDMI can.) 1. **On the TV**, open **Apps** and type `1 2 3 4 5` on the remote. Turn **Developer mode** on, type your computer's IP address in **Host PC IP**, and restart the TV. 2. **On your computer**, download [TizenBrew Installer](https://github.com/reisxd/TizenBrewInstaller/releases/latest), the community's installer for Samsung TVs, open it and connect to your TV. 3. **Install from GitHub:** type `simbasjungles/free-my-tv`. On 2023 and newer TVs it asks you to sign in to your Samsung account once, to sign the app for your TV. 4. **Straight to it:** in the TV's settings, under Start Screen Options, turn on **Autorun Last App**: the TV turns on into Free My TV. This build takes your city from the TV's time zone. For your exact city and the trending picks, build it with your own `config.properties` and [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key): open the folder in Claude Code and say *"Install Free My TV on my Samsung TV at 192.168.1.50. I live in Lisbon."* It sets up Samsung's tools, and on 2023 and newer TVs you sign in to your Samsung account in the browser to make the certificate. Your signed build installs with `python3 tizen/install.py 192.168.1.50`, which needs only Python: no Tizen Studio, and no Rosetta on Apple Silicon Macs. ## Settings The first values come from `config.properties`, created by the first build (Google TV, LG and Samsung use the same file). Most of them can also be changed on the TV, in *Free My TV* → *Home Settings*, and the TV's choice wins: | Key | What it does | Default | |---|---|---| | `tmdb_key` | Your free TMDB key, for the picks | empty | | `tmdb_region` | Your country (two letters): which titles are on which app | `US` | | `watchmode_key` | Optional, free [Watchmode](https://api.watchmode.com/) key: a pick opens the title's page in its app | empty | | `latitude`, `longitude` | Your city, for the weather and the sunset | New York | | `city` | The name on the weather card | `Weather` | | `hide_animation` | Leave cartoons and anime out of the picks | `false` | | `language` | `auto` (follows the TV), or a language with a [translation](#translations) (`en`, `pt`, `es`, `de`, `ru`, `fr`, `ja`…) | `auto` | | `show_crypto` | Show Binance crypto prices on home and screensaver | `true` | | `currency` | Crypto prices in `USD`, `EUR`, `BRL`… | `USD` | | `temperature` | `C`, `F` or `auto` | `auto` | | `theme` | `auto` (dark from sunset to sunrise), `light` or `dark` | `auto` | | `disable_assistant` | Also turn off Google Assistant | `false` | | `hide_services` | Streaming services to leave out of the picks even when their app is on the TV (`netflix`, `prime`, `disney`…), comma separated; for apps the TV ships that you don't subscribe to. Google TV only | empty | | `hide_apps` | Apps to leave out of the shelf, All Apps and the picks, by id or name (part of it), comma separated; for apps the TV ships that can't be uninstalled, like Samsung's built-in Netflix. LG and Samsung only | empty | | `shelf_apps` | The shelf's apps in this order, by id or name (part of it), comma separated; changing it wins once over the shelf picked on the TV. On Samsung, a whole app id also brings an app the TV leaves out of its list, like one installed in Developer Mode. LG and Samsung only | empty | Changed something? Run `./build.sh` and install again. Keep `freemytv.keystore`: updates are signed with it. ### The TMDB key Free, and it takes two minutes: create an account at [themoviedb.org](https://www.themoviedb.org/signup), then open [Settings → API](https://www.themoviedb.org/settings/api) and request a developer key. Paste the *API Read Access Token* (or the *API Key*) after `tmdb_key=`. It's your key: `config.properties` stays out of git. ### Opening a title, not just its app (optional) With a free [Watchmode](https://api.watchmode.com/) key (`watchmode_key=` in `config.properties`), a pick opens its own page in the streaming app instead of the app's home. The free plan (2,500 credits a month) is enough: each title costs two requests the first time and is remembered after that. It works where the app takes the title's web address (tested: Prime Video and JioHotstar); where it doesn't, the pick just opens the app, as without a key. ### Your own photos (optional) On Google TV and Android TV, with the TV connected over adb (see *Install*), send photos or whole folders from your computer: ```bash python3 tools/photos.py beach.jpg hills.jpg Holidays/ ``` They land in the app's own folder on the TV (no permission needed); on Android 11, which keeps adb out of other apps' folders, they go through Free My TV itself. The next time the home screen, the screensaver or Free My TV's settings open, the app imports each one: turned upright, cropped to 16:9, resized for the TV and saved without its GPS and other tags; what was sent is then deleted. The screensaver shows them in the order you sent them, instead of the picks' photos; without a TMDB key, one of them is the home screen's background, a new one every hour. *Home Settings* → *My Photos*: the arrows turn them on or off, OK removes them. Up to 100; JPEG, PNG and WebP, and HEIC on Android 9 and newer. ## Going back On the TV: *Free My TV* → *Home Screen* → *Original*. The factory home screen, screensaver and every app come back exactly as they were. If the new home screen ever crashes three times in five minutes, it switches back by itself. To remove it for good, switch to *Original* first, then uninstall *Free My TV* (Settings → Apps). Uninstalled it while it was on? Install it again and pick *Original*: the list of what it turned off is kept in the TV's settings, so everything comes back. ## What it changes - It becomes the home screen and the screensaver. - It turns off, without uninstalling: - the stock home screen and screensaver; - Google TV's recovery home, Play Games and YouTube Music; - on TCL TVs, the TCL Channel, messages, store demo, hotel menu, manuals, mirroring and logging apps; - on Philco TVs, AI PONT (promo channels and app downloads) and the manual; - on Multilaser TVs, Anoki's screen-content recognition (ACR), the store demo and the manual; - on KTC-made TVs (NextStar), Anoki's screen-content recognition (ACR), the store demo and the manual; - Google Assistant, only with `disable_assistant=true`. - On Google TV, the Assistant's results for films and shows come from Google TV's home app, which is off in Free My TV mode: asking it to play a show can end in "Sorry, I don't understand", and a search can show only YouTube videos. Opening apps, questions and apps' own voice search (YouTube's, for one) still work; *Original* brings it all back. - On TCL TVs, the remote's Netflix, YouTube and Prime buttons keep working through a small accessibility service that only reads those buttons. Pick what each one opens in *Free My TV* → *Remote Buttons*; *Original* turns the service off. On Vestel-made TVs (F&U and other store brands) and Xiaomi (Formovie) projectors the same goes for the Netflix button, and on KTC-made TVs (NextStar) for the Tabii button. On Sony TVs, the BRAVIA CORE, Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video, YouTube and Crunchyroll buttons (and Google Play, on remotes that have it) can each open the app you pick, or keep Sony's default. On Xiaomi TVs whose remote has a Mi button instead of Home, that button opens Free My TV instead of PatchWall (or, if you pick it, PatchWall as before, or another app). On Xiaomi TVs sold in Russia, the same goes for the Okko, VK, Rutube, KION, Wink and IVI buttons, which keep Xiaomi's default until you pick another app. On Hisense TVs, the Prime Video, YouTube, Disney+, All Apps, Settings and profile buttons, which Google TV's home screen answered, open what you pick (All Apps opens Free My TV's own; Netflix stays with the TV). - On HY300 projectors, whose stock home screen was the only way to them, the bottom drawer gets *Keystone* (keystone, zoom and projection mode) and *Screen Mirroring* (the projector's Miracast receiver), and HDMI opens through the projector's own player. - *Free My TV* → *Sleep Timer* turns the TV off after 5 minutes to 4 hours, with the minutes left over any app (top center, or the corner you pick). It presses the remote's Sleep key through the TV's own ADB, so it works in Free My TV mode; *Original* stops it. - Picture, sound, inputs, remote pairing, Google services and the Play Store are on a protected list, checked before every change, and so are Android's own pieces and factory menus. Before anything goes off, the TV is asked whether its inputs or its remote's Input key depend on it; those stay on. - On Google TV, the setup app goes off before the stock home screen and comes back after it, so its recovery screen never takes over the Home button in between. - Apps that saved a Wi-Fi network are never turned off, since Android would erase the network. If the TV's first setup saved yours, the switch asks you to forget the network and connect again in Settings first (saved networks out of range don't show there; Claude Code can remove them). ## Any TV Free My TV runs on Google TV and Android TV: TCL, Sony, Hisense, Philips, Xiaomi, Vestel-made TVs (F&U), KTC-made TVs (NextStar) and more, plus streamers like Chromecast with Google TV, the Google TV Streamer, onn 4K and NVIDIA Shield. And on [LG](#lg-tvs-webos) and [Samsung](#samsung-tvs-tizen) TVs, as an app. **Any other TV:** plug a Google TV streamer into HDMI and free that one. Same steps, same home screen. **A different brand or model:** ask Claude. Free My TV is made to be adapted by AI. Open the folder in Claude Code and say *"set it up for my Sony"*: it reads your TV, finds its home screen and its promo apps, updates the lists below and walks you through a test. [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) tells it how. | What | Where | |---|---| | Apps to turn off | `DEBLOAT` in [`HomeMode.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeMode.java) | | Apps never to touch | `PROTECTED` in the same file | | Apps on the shelf | `SHELF` in [`HomeApps.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeApps.java) | | Your brand's live TV app | `LIVE_TV_APPS` in the same file | ## Make it yours It's your code, and Claude Code finds its way around it. Try: - *"Add Crunchyroll to the shelf."* - *"Show the prices in euros."* - *"Add Catalan."* - *"Switch to the night look an hour after sunset."* ## How it works - **A plain Android app, no Gradle, no libraries.** [`build.sh`](build.sh) runs aapt2 → javac → d8 → zipalign → apksigner and makes a 2 MB APK. - **It uses the TV's own ADB, from inside the TV.** The app connects to `127.0.0.1:5555` with its own key (that's the *Allow USB debugging?* prompt) and runs the same commands you would: `cmd package set-home-activity`, `settings put secure screensaver_components`, `pm disable-user`. Nothing listens to the network. - **Drawn by hand on one Canvas**, with Android 13 shaders for the frosted glass and the sky (plain fills on Android 8 to 12, with lighter shadows and no GPU layers on 8 to 11 for their older GPUs). - **A safety net.** A watchdog in a separate process brings back the stock home screen after three crashes in five minutes, and a boot check keeps your choice after TV updates. - **On LG and Samsung, the same design in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript** ([`web/`](web)), written for the Chromium of older TVs, with no frameworks. [`webos/build.py`](webos/build.py) packs it with `config.properties` into an `.ipk` without LG's tools, and [`webos/install.py`](webos/install.py) installs it through Developer Mode; on LG it lists and opens apps through the TV's own service bus (Luna), as LG's launcher does. [`tizen/build.py`](tizen/build.py) packs the same app into a Samsung `.wgt`, which uses Tizen's web APIs for the apps and the inputs. To preview it on a computer: `python3 webos/build.py --preview`, then open `out/webos/index.html` (a stand-in lists sample apps). - **Data** from TMDB (trending titles, new releases and which app streams what in your country), Open-Meteo (forecast, sunrise and sunset), and optionally Binance (24-hour prices when `show_crypto=true`). | File | What it is | |---|---| | [`HomeView.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeView.java) | The home screen | | [`HomeMode.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeMode.java) | Switching between Free My TV and Original | | [`Adb.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Adb.java) | The TV's own ADB, from inside the TV | | [`Recs.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Recs.java) | The picks (TMDB) | | [`HomeData.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeData.java) | Weather and prices | | [`HomeApps.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeApps.java) | The shelf, inputs and All Apps | | [`DreamView.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/DreamView.java) | The screensaver | | [`SettingsActivity.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/SettingsActivity.java) | The settings screen (the app's icon) | | [`Prefs.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Prefs.java) | Settings changed on the TV | | [`RemoteKeys.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/RemoteKeys.java) | The remote's app buttons (TCL, Sony, Xiaomi and others) | | [`Watchdog.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Watchdog.java) | The safety net | | [`web/home.js`](web/home.js) | The home screen on LG TVs | | [`web/tv.js`](web/tv.js) | The TV's apps and inputs, on LG and Samsung | | [`webos/build.py`](webos/build.py), [`webos/install.py`](webos/install.py) | The LG app package and its install | | [`tizen/build.py`](tizen/build.py) | The Samsung app package | The website ([freemytv.io](https://freemytv.io)) is in [`docs/`](docs): plain HTML, CSS and JS on GitHub Pages. ## Translations On Google TV, LG and Samsung, each language is one file, [`app/assets/i18n/.json`](app/assets/i18n), keyed by the English text in the code. *Automatic* follows the TV's language and uses any language that has a file (English otherwise); *Home Settings* → *Language* lists them all. Today: English, Portuguese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Finnish, Czech, Romanian, Turkish, Russian, Ukrainian, Greek, Japanese, Korean, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Hindi, Indonesian, Vietnamese and Thai. Portuguese, Spanish, German, Russian, Thai and Turkish were translated by hand and are the reference (fix them by hand); the others were machine-made, and corrections from native speakers are welcome. - **Add a language:** `python3 tools/translate.py --new ca`, then fill `app/assets/i18n/ca.json` by hand, or with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set, `python3 tools/translate.py --fill --lang ca` (only the strings go to the API). - **After changing text in the code:** `python3 tools/translate.py` lists what each language lacks; `--fill` translates only that, `--prune` drops strings the code no longer uses. Run `python3 tools/translate.py --check` to validate all catalogues without writing files. - Text built at runtime has placeholders (`"{n} min ago"`), so each language puts the words in its own order. A key like `"unit|Automatic"` is the same English in another place, where a language may need another word. - Counts have plural forms: `"plural|one:{n} season|other:{n} seasons"` is translated with one form per plural category the language uses (Russian `"one:{n} сезон|few:{n} сезона|many:{n} сезонов|other:{n} сезона"`, Japanese just `"other:{n}シーズン"`), and Android's plural rules pick the one for each number. - **Limits:** right-to-left languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian) would need the layout mirrored, so they aren't there yet. Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Hindi are drawn with the TV's system font (Inter has no such letters). ## Privacy No accounts, no analytics, no tracking. The app talks to TMDB, Open-Meteo (with the coordinates you set, or your time zone's main city), and Binance only when `show_crypto=true`, and Watchmode only when you set a `watchmode_key`. Your settings stay on your computer and your TV. ## Credits - Built with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code). - The LG version builds on what [@danielthejoker18](https://github.com/danielthejoker18) found in [FreeMyTvWebOS](https://github.com/danielthejoker18/FreeMyTvWebOS) (MIT): installing through Developer Mode and opening apps through the TV's service bus. - On Samsung TVs it installs with [TizenBrew Installer](https://github.com/reisxd/TizenBrewInstaller) by [@reisxd](https://github.com/reisxd). - This product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by [TMDB](https://www.themoviedb.org/). - Links to the titles in the streaming apps by [Watchmode](https://api.watchmode.com/). - Weather data by [Open-Meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/) (CC BY 4.0). Prices from the [Binance](https://www.binance.com/) public API. - Icons: [Material Symbols](https://fonts.google.com/icons) (Apache 2.0). Font: [Inter](https://rsms.me/inter/) (SIL OFL 1.1). Coin logos: [cryptocurrency-icons](https://github.com/spothq/cryptocurrency-icons) (CC0). Samsung app logos: [Simple Icons](https://simpleicons.org) (CC0). - Not affiliated with Google, TCL, LG, Samsung or any streaming service. App names and logos belong to their owners. ## License [MIT](LICENSE). Fork it, change it, ship it.

title: Jakeschincariol/replica-skill
author: Jakeschincariol
body:
# The Replica skill

Eleven Claude skills that clone any app. Free, MIT, no signup, no API key,
nothing to connect.

One reverse-engineers the app you want to clone. One rebuilds it. One tests it
for bugs. And one is the Entrepreneur: it reads what the app's users hate and
fixes it in yours, so you have an app you can sell.

In between, the others plan the stack and the database, rebuild the design
system, wire up auth and payments, score your clone against the original, give
it a name and a brand of its own, write the landing page and the store
listing, and put it live on your domain.

**It rebuilds what an app does, never what it owns.** Features and flows,
clean-room style. Not its code, its logo, its copy or its content. The
fine print is at the bottom, and the skills enforce it.

## Install

Paste this into Claude:

```
https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/replica-skill

install skill
```

Or as a plugin, in Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add Jakeschincariol/replica-skill
/plugin install replica-skill@replica-skill
```

Claude Code namespaces plugin skills, so installed as a plugin they show up as
`/replica-skill:replica-recon` and so on. Copy the folders instead if you want
plain `/replica-recon`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/replica-skill.git
cp -r replica-skill/replica-* ~/.claude/skills/
```

Project-local instead of global: copy the same folders into your repo's
`.claude/skills/`. No Claude Code at all? Paste any single `SKILL.md` at the
top of a chat and it runs as a mode. You lose the Python tools, but the
method works.

The tools need Python 3.8 or newer. Nothing to pip install.

## The eleven

| command | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/replica-recon` | Reverse-engineers any app: screens, flows, components, data model. From public pages, screenshots, store listings and your own account. |
| `/replica-architect` | Plans the stack, database schema and API for your clone. |
| `/replica-design` | Rebuilds the design system: colours, type, spacing, components. As tokens, with your own assets. |
| `/replica-build` | Rebuilds the app screen by screen from the recon map. |
| `/replica-backend` | Auth, database, payments and integrations. |
| `/replica-test` | Clicks through every flow and tests it for bugs. |
| `/replica-diff` | Compares your clone against the original. A parity score and what is missing. |
| `/replica-entrepreneur` | Reads what the app's users hate in real reviews and turns it into fixes and a positioning angle. |
| `/replica-brand` | Names and rebrands your version so it is yours. |
| `/replica-launch` | Landing page, pricing and App Store listing. |
| `/replica-deploy` | Ships it live on your own domain. |

## How to use it

Run them in order. Each one reads what the last one wrote, in a `replica/`
folder in your project.

```
recon -> architect -> design -> build -> backend -> test -> diff -> entrepreneur -> brand -> launch -> deploy
```

An example: cloning a scheduling app, the kind where you share a link and
people book a time with you.

1. **`/replica-recon`** with the app's URL. It reads the help center, the
   pricing page, the store listing and public walkthroughs, and you click
   through your own account with it. Out comes `replica/recon.md`: 18
   screens, 7 flows (guest books a meeting, host sets availability, guest
   reschedules...), the components, an inferred data model (users, event
   types, availability, bookings) and `features.csv`. The partner
   marketplace is marked out of scope: that is their network, not a feature.
2. **`/replica-architect`** picks Next.js, Postgres, Stripe and Resend, writes
   the schema (with a constraint so two guests can never book the same slot)
   and orders the build: the booking flow end to end first.
3. **`/replica-design`** measures the screenshots into tokens: colour roles,
   type scale, 8px spacing, the date picker and slot button specs. Open
   icons, an open font, your own words.
4. **`/replica-build`** builds the shell, then the booking flow, then every
   screen with all its states, ticking off `features.csv` as it goes.
5. **`/replica-backend`** adds sign up, Google Calendar through Google's own
   API with your keys, Stripe for paid bookings, reminder emails.
6. **`/replica-test`** writes a test plan from the 7 flows, Playwright specs
   for the happy paths and edge cases (time zones, a slot taken mid-booking,
   double submit), and logs bugs by severity until no S1 or S2 is open.
7. **`/replica-diff`** scores it. Features 86, all must-haves done, booking
   page layout 91. Missing: round-robin for teams, the website embed.
8. **`/replica-entrepreneur`** reads 140 real reviews across the App Store,
   G2, Capterra and Reddit. Top complaints: per-seat price jumps, no text
   reminders, guests confused by time zones. Each with counts and linked
   quotes. Fix plan: flat pricing, SMS reminders, a time zone confirm step.
   Angle: booking links for small teams that hate per-seat pricing.
9. **`/replica-brand`** names it (with the trademark and domain checks to
   run), gives it a new palette, a logo brief and a voice, then sweeps the
   codebase until nothing of the original is left.
10. **`/replica-launch`** writes the landing page around the angle, sets
    pricing against the original's public page, and lints the store listing.
11. **`/replica-deploy`** runs the preflight (tests, parity, sweep, listing),
    sets up production, gives you the DNS records for your domain, and ships
    it when you say go.

You can also run any one on its own. `/replica-entrepreneur` on an app you
are only thinking about cloning is a good way to find out if you should.

## The tools

Six of them, all standard-library Python. None touch the network.

```bash
python3 replica-diff/imgdiff.py original.png clone.png --out diff.png   # layout diff, ignores colour
python3 replica-diff/parity.py replica/features.csv                     # parity score + missing list
python3 replica-entrepreneur/reviews.py replica/reviews.csv             # what users hate, ranked, linked
python3 replica-design/contrast.py replica/design/tokens.json           # WCAG contrast on your tokens
python3 replica-brand/sweep.py . --avoid "Original App"                 # anything of the original left?
python3 replica-launch/listing.py replica/launch/listing.json           # store limits + copycat checks
```

**`imgdiff.py`** reads PNGs with no libraries, turns both screenshots into
edge maps and compares where things are, so your new colours do not count
against you. It tells you which regions differ, in the original's pixels.

**`parity.py`** weights must, should and could, counts partial as half, and
never scores what you left out on purpose or what you added. Missing
must-haves means not shippable, and it says so.

**`reviews.py`** drops every review without a link. Every quote it prints is
copied from a row you gave it, with that row's URL. Themes with under three
reviews or one source are marked thin.

**`sweep.py`** finds the original's name, domain and colours anywhere in your
code, including inside identifiers like `OriginalAppEmbed`, and blocks the
deploy until it is clean.

**`listing.py`** checks App Store and Google Play limits, ranking claims in
the title, wasted keyword characters, and the original's name anywhere in
your listing.

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

## Fine print

**It rebuilds functionality and UX patterns, clean-room style.** It studies
what the app does and how people move through it, then writes everything
fresh. It never copies the target's source code, proprietary assets, logos,
trademarks, copy or private APIs.

**It only reads what you are allowed to read.** Public pages and your own
account. It never scrapes behind a login or against a site's terms, never
logs into anyone else's account, and never gets past a paywall. If your
account's terms forbid using it to build a competitor, it says so and sticks
to public sources.

**It always rebrands before launch.** New name, new palette, new logo, new
words. `/replica-deploy` will not ship until the sweep is clean.

**"Clone any app" means the features and the flow.** Not the content, the
network or the licences an app owns. You can rebuild a music app's player,
playlists and sharing. You cannot clone its catalogue.

**No guarantee of a "perfect" clone.** Results depend on how complex the app
is. A booking tool is weeks. A spreadsheet engine is not. `/replica-recon`
sizes it honestly before you start, and `/replica-diff` gives you a real
number, not a vibe.

**The Entrepreneur never makes things up.** No invented reviews, quotes or
numbers. Every claim has a link, and the sample size is stated.

**Check before you sell.** Run the trademark checks `/replica-brand` lists,
read the terms of anything you used, and talk to a lawyer before launch if
there is money on the line. This is not legal advice.
